Cory Doctorow: willing science fiction into fact
This article is more than 17 years old
Damien G Walter
The activist-novelist explains to Damien G Walter how he hopes his writing will change tomorrow's world
Tue 25 Nov 2008 07.21 EST
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google
C
ory Doctorow's office lies behind a featureless, black security door in a north London side street, deep in a converted post-industrial warehouse, down echoing corridors and concrete stairways. It's an appropriately "underground" headquarters for the activist-novelist, who is explaining to me why he's not interested in predicting the future using
science fiction
, but influencing it.
"I'm a presentist," he says, smiling broadly as he leans back in his chair. "All science fiction writers, whether they admit it or not, are writing metaphorically about the present. To extrapolate the future is really to comment on the now."
His latest novel, Little Brother, is a counter-cultural manual for modern youth, which follows a tech-savvy teen, Marcus, as he takes on a sinister Department for Homeland Security in the wake of a terrorist attack on San Francisco. Full of handy tips for anyone trying to avoid the prying eyes of the state – use a metal wallet to carry your cards, hide your sensitive files behind a dummy operating system with a dummy password – it's set in a fictional future so close as to be almost with us already.
"The job of a science fiction writer, historically, has been to understand how technology and social factors interact," he says, "how technology is changing society. An activist's job is to try to direct that change."
This time his message is aimed at the teenage readers who wear the kind of skater jeans and T-shirt combination Doctorow is sporting today. "If you don't read the Anarchist's Cookbook when you are 16 you have no soul," he says. "If you are still reading it when you are 36 you have no brain." (He himself is 37, but if he's abandoned anarchism, he's clearly not settling into a conservative middle age.)
"My hope is that Little Brother is a verb and not a noun, that it's a thing you do, not just a book you read," he continues. "That's where thinking about the future and influencing the future converge."
This desire to understand the future, so as to change the here and now is one he shares with some of science fiction's greatest writers, including writers he cites as influences such as William Gibson, Neal Stephenson and Bruce Sterling. It's a path he's been following since 1992, when he took part in the six-week Clarion science fiction workshop taught by another science fiction writer engaged with the world as it is today, James Patrick Kelly.
"[Kelly] called me an asshole and told me my work at the time was merely verbal pyrotechnics without any depth," says Doctorow. "He told me I needed to learn to sit down at a keyboard and open a vein."
That was advice it would take Doctorow a five-year bout of writer's block to fully process, but it's put him in a position where his fiction is gaining the kind of audience where it can start to influence opinion.
"Communities are king," he explains. "If a book is adopted as an identity marker by a social group, it earns a secondary use that goes beyond reading to participating in the community that goes around it."
As one of the founders of the
Boing Boing
blog, and a columnist for the Guardian's technology site, Doctorow is no stranger to contemporary debates on internet security, electronic copyright and privacy. A fellow of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, Doctorow also serves on the board of the Open Rights Group and the Participatory Culture Foundation. But despite his concerns over government plans to monitor electronic communications, he remains positive about the net's potential. He himself has used the net to build a large audience for his fiction online by releasing it for free under creative commons licences on his website,
Craphound.com
.
According to Doctorow, the low cost of failure on the web makes it easier than ever for people who want to "do interesting things", whatever they might be.
"The important thing that the internet does is dramatically lower the cost of all forms of collective action, from Wikipedia to al-Qaida," he says.
The internet also raises much more prosaic dangers than the "awfully uncommon" threat of terrorism. Doctorow's first novel, Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom, painted the picture of a 22nd century world of theme parks run by informal "adhocracies" where money has been replaced by "Whuffie" – a constantly updated measure of reputation. It's an idea put into practise now by social websites such as Digg, but Doctorow is unconvinced by some of the wilder claims for its liberating potential.
"I am actually a deep Whuffie sceptic," he explains. "The problem is the same as with cash economics, the lack of social mobility and a winner-takes-all economy. It is also powerfully normative and punishing of minority viewpoints." Far from propagating new ideas, the internet can work to suppress them, especially if they fail to gather popularity. "Pretty much all transformational ideas are challenging to the status quo," he continues. "A society that doesn't protect unpopular ideas is one that is probably doomed."
